text: It seems to work is not a test plan -- it's a guess dressed up as confidence. A real test plan is a table of specific, checkable claims: given this exact input, this exact result should happen, and anything else is a defect, not a judgment call. For this workstream, that means three categories -- Domain Separation, integration error handling, and one deliberately messy edge case.

Domain Separation runs three for three. A Lakeshore agent sees only Lakeshore work. A Meridian executive sees the rollup across all three domains. A St. Catherine's agent trying to open a Lakeshore record by direct sys_id gets blocked by Domain Separation's own access rules. Integration error handling runs two for two as well -- a failed API call logs and returns nothing instead of writing bad data, and a repeated worker record updates in place instead of duplicating.

Then one case fails. A Prairie View director's user record was created manually in the global domain weeks before this integration existed. The sync runs, recognizes her as an existing worker, and refreshes her name and department -- but her domain stays wrong. Her next request routes to the corporate default queue instead of Prairie View's own. Reading upsertWorker line by line finds it immediately: the domain assignment only happens inside the new-record branch.

An existing record's domain is simply never touched again after its first sync -- a quiet assumption that held for every brand-new record and broke for the one record that predated the integration. The fix moves that one line outside the conditional, so every run, new record or existing one, gets its domain set explicitly.

Rerunning the exact same test case confirms the fix directly: her record is corrected on the next sync, and her next request routes to the right queue. That's what a real test plan buys -- a found defect and a confirmed fix, not an assumption. Lesson 18 writes up what shipped, how to roll it back if it doesn't hold, and why, as a real deployment record.
